questions.q: Why is it important to check whether the entire depreciation book ran successfully before investigating one specific asset?
options: Because a whole-book failure and a single-asset exclusion from a successful run are very different tickets requiring different investigations
It isn't important — always investigate the single asset first
Because depreciation always runs for the whole book or not at all
Because Oracle doesn't allow partial depreciation runs
questions.explain: Confirming the scope first (whole book vs. one asset) directs the investigation correctly — here, every other asset depreciated normally, isolating the problem to one asset.

questions.q: What was the actual reason the stamping press had no depreciation?
options: The depreciation method was set incorrectly
The accounting period was closed
The asset's Mass Additions line was on hold (missing asset category) and had never been posted into the active asset register
The asset was flagged as fully depreciated
questions.explain: The asset never became an active, depreciating asset because its Mass Additions line was stuck on hold due to a missing required asset category.

questions.q: Why can't an asset still sitting in the Mass Additions queue depreciate?
options: It can depreciate; the queue status is irrelevant
Depreciation only applies to assets that have been posted into the active asset register — a queued line isn't yet an asset
Mass Additions assets always depreciate at double the normal rate
Queue status only affects Payables, not Fixed Assets
questions.explain: An asset only becomes eligible for depreciation once it has been posted out of Mass Additions into the active asset register.

questions.q: Why did the fix need to address the asset's in-service date specifically?
options: In-service date has no effect on depreciation calculations
Because Oracle requires manually entering a depreciation amount
Because the in-service date determines the asset's physical location
Because the asset was actually placed in service in August, so depreciation needed to catch up for the missed month rather than starting fresh from the current month
questions.explain: Since the press was actually in service starting in August, correcting the in-service date allows depreciation to catch up for the missed month rather than only starting going forward.

questions.q: What was missing that caused the Mass Additions line to go on hold?
options: A required asset category assignment that Prepare Mass Additions could not derive automatically
A supplier bank account
An invoice number
A purchase order
questions.explain: The line lacked an asset category, which Prepare Mass Additions needs to derive the expense account; without it, the line is held rather than posted.
